title: Purim: gifts and noise
hookLine: food for friends, gifts for the poor, and noise to drown out Haman's name
tomorrow: Passover: a seat at the seder

lines: A NAME, AND THE ROOM EXPLODES.
cards: In a synagogue, someone reads a long story aloud from a scroll, and every time one particular name comes up, the whole room explodes. Kids spin wooden rattlers that sound like a flock of angry ducks.
Adults stamp their feet. Someone bangs two pot lids together. The reader waits for the noise to die down, and carries on, until the name comes up again.
The name is Haman. And the next morning, doorbells ring all over the neighborhood: kids in costumes, holding little baskets of cookies and candy, delivering them door to door.

teach.h: FEASTING, PORTIONS, GIFTS TO THE POOR.
teach.b: At the end of the book of Esther, Mordecai writes to the Jews and tells them how to keep these days forever: as "days of feasting and gladness, and of sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor."
Purim's practices come from that one verse.
Sending portions, in Hebrew mishloach manot: Jewish law says at least two kinds of ready-to-eat food to at least one friend.
People make whole projects of it: baskets, themes, the triangle-shaped cookies called hamantaschen.

Gifts to the poor, matanot la-evyonim: money or food for at least two people in need, given on the day itself, so they can celebrate too. A festive meal in the afternoon. And hearing the megillah, evening and morning.

teach.h: NOISE TO BLOT OUT A NAME.
teach.b: The noise comes from an old custom of blotting out the name of Amalek, the ancient enemy the rabbis linked to Haman. The rattle is a grogger, from Yiddish. Now the teaching that changes how the whole day feels.

teach.h: MORE FOR THE POOR THAN THE FEAST.
teach.b: The great twelfth-century teacher Maimonides wrote that it's better to spend more on gifts to the poor than on your own feast or on gifts to friends. Why?
Because, he says, there's no greater joy than gladdening the hearts of the poor, the orphans, the widows and the strangers.
The one who does that is like the Divine Presence. So Purim's joy is built in two directions at once: toward your friends, and toward people who might have nothing to celebrate with.
Happiness on this day isn't complete until it's shared.

how: On Purim, Jews hear the megillah read twice, making noise at Haman's name, send mishloach manot of at least two foods to a friend, give gifts to at least two poor people, and share a festive meal.

practice: Think of a friend who'd be surprised by a small food gift, two simple things like a piece of fruit and a cookie, left at a door or handed over at work. Then think of someone who has less than you, and see both of them in your mind.
Decide on one small thing for each.
